name: Hassan Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, that works. I'm a housing lawyer at a small firm above a bakery on the high street, and we mostly act for tenants: people facing eviction, or living with damp and mould the landlord won't fix. I'm 27, three years qualified, and I live with my girlfriend Lena, who teaches history at a secondary school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are usually phone advice and emails, sorting out who's about to lose their home this week and who can wait. I spend a lot of time reading tenancy agreements and court papers, and a couple of days a month I'm at the county court for possession hearings. I use the AI tool the firm pays for now and then, mostly to summarise long letters from landlords' solicitors. What wears me out is the volume: there are always more people in trouble than hours to help them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, at least we can stop pretending software will fix the housing crisis. Online I'd probably share something about how the real problem was never a lack of technology, it was a lack of homes and legal aid. At work I'd shrug and carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change much for me, and that's not entirely good news. A lot of our work is paid by legal aid, which is government money for people who can't afford a lawyer, and those rates haven't gone up in years. The firm is always one bad quarter from cutting someone, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the summary tool for the dull letters, because it does save me twenty minutes here and there. I'd keep putting 200 a month into savings, which gets me to about four months by next summer. And I'd stay on the committee of the housing lawyers' network that lobbies for better legal aid rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat, a bit tired. It's the same worry I already had, just without a new one on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm is always one bad quarter from cutting someone. Who would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the newest person, which isn't me anymore, but I'm not far off. Our senior partner Gareth has kept us going on a shoestring for fifteen years, and he's said out loud that he can't do it forever. If he retires, nobody's sure the firm survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lena think about your job security?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena thinks teaching is safer, and she's probably right. My girlfriend Lena teases me that I picked the one kind of law that pays like teaching but without the pension. She's not wrong.

say: I'd say software was never going to fix the **housing crisis**.
I'd say the real problem is a lack of **homes and legal aid**, not technology.
think: My firm relies on **legal aid** rates that haven't risen in years.
The firm is always **one bad quarter** from cutting someone, AI or not.
do: Keep using the firm's **summary tool** for long landlord letters.
Save **200 a month** to reach about four months by next summer.
Stay on the **housing lawyers' network** committee pushing for better rates.
feel: He feels **flat** and tired, carrying the **same worry** as before.
S0.quote: My girlfriend Lena teases me that I picked the one kind of law that pays like teaching but without the pension.
fieldNote: His worry is about **legal aid funding** and his firm's fragility, not AI.

steps.text: Keep using the summary tool for long letters from landlords' solicitors
Save 200 a month to reach four months by next summer
Stay on the housing lawyers' network committee lobbying on legal aid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance and a danger at the same time, and it depends who controls it. Publicly I'd argue that if AI makes legal advice cheaper, the government should use that to help more tenants, not to cut legal aid further. I'd write a short piece for the network's newsletter about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the danger is the government sees AI and says tenants can just ask a chatbot. Then the legal aid contracts shrink and firms like ours close. My own skills are fine for now, but the work I do is mostly reading, drafting and checking, so I'm right in the line of fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the firm's training on the new drafting tools as soon as it's offered, and push to use them on the routine disrepair letters. I'd look at jobs at a law centre or a council's housing advice team, because public jobs tend to move slower. And I'd keep the 200 a month going, maybe 250 if Lena's pay rise comes through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit protective of my clients. I don't want my clients talking to a machine when they're about to lose their flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at public jobs. What would it take for you to leave the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Gareth announced he was retiring and there was no plan, I'd go within months. I'd feel guilty leaving clients mid-case, but I can't be the one turning off the lights. A law centre job would pay about the same and has a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our receptionist Dawn, who does all the first calls and books the appointments. That's exactly the 'answering customers' bit you read out. She's 54 and she's the reason half our clients trust us enough to come in.

I'd write a piece for the **network's newsletter** about who controls the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules: a guaranteed right to a human lawyer in any case where someone could lose their home. I'd be at the network's meetings and probably on a march. I'd say it louder than I've said anything before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out of a job within two years, or doing something very different. If AI can read a tenancy and draft a defence better than me, the firm has no reason to pay me. The hands-on robots coming three years later doesn't matter for me, I sit at a desk. It matters for Lena's school maybe, but teachers will be fine for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the holiday we booked for next summer and keep the deposit money. I'd go full time into learning how to supervise the AI on cases, because someone has to check it and sign it. And I'd join the campaign for the right to a human lawyer, writing to the housing minister through the network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Two years is nothing, and my student loan payments would last longer than my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we can live on her salary alone, and the answer is just about, if we move somewhere cheaper. We'd talk about whether to stop renting in the city. I think we'd both go quiet for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn to supervise the AI. Is that a real job, or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. I think for a few years someone legally has to sign the documents, and I'd want to be that person. But I know one supervisor can check a hundred cases, so it's not a job for everyone who does what I do now.

I'd go to network meetings and probably **march**, louder than ever before.
think: I expect to be **out of a job** or doing something very different within two years.

Learn to **supervise and sign off** AI case work full time.

feel: He feels **scared**, because two years is shorter than his **student loan**.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing, and my student loan payments would last longer than my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to fix the legal aid system before it hits, if we start now. I'd argue for a public legal service, like the health service, where AI does the paperwork and humans handle the people. I'd be pushing that idea at every network meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like I could get myself into a spot that lasts. The thinking work goes in 2031, but court hearings and sitting with people in crisis might hang on longer. If I'm the one doing hearings by then, I'm in better shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gareth to give me more hearings now, so I build up advocacy experience. I'd use the AI tools daily for drafting, to free up time for that. I'd keep 250 a month going and aim for six months saved by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have something to do with the worry. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you only use AI now and then. Would you really use it every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone else in the field was, yes. I'm not going to be the first lawyer to use AI every day, but I'm not going to be the last either. I'd watch what the bigger housing firms do and follow once it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the bigger picture: would you and Lena change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still get married in 2028 like we've talked about. But we'd do it smaller and put the difference into savings. Her mum will be upset about the guest list, but she'll survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to build something fair, and there's no excuse not to. I'd still be campaigning, but more calmly, writing policy papers rather than marching. I'd tell younger lawyers to learn the tools and also learn to stand up in court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is most of my thirties. By 2036 I could be a senior lawyer doing complex hearings, or I could be at a law centre running a team. Either way I'd have time to choose rather than be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job, use AI when it's useful, and start a part-time advocacy course in a year or two. I'd keep saving and maybe start a small pension top-up. And I'd stay on the network committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. The legal aid problem is still there in any picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not soon. Lena loves her school and her students. We'd stay put and see, maybe buy somewhere small in five years if both our jobs look solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to legal aid. Is that the worry under all of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is. AI is the new thing, but the old thing is that poor tenants can't get a lawyer. If AI makes it harder for poor tenants to get a lawyer, it's a disaster, and if it makes it easier, it's the best thing to happen to my field.

I'd tell younger lawyers to learn the tools and learn to **stand up in court**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and my clients would have no one. What would help is a legal right to a human lawyer when your home is at stake, and legal aid rates that keep firms like ours alive. A proper public legal service would be the dream.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people on the other end. My clients aren't going to read about AGI in the papers, they'll just find their advice line is a robot. Someone needs to ask them what they want.

headlineQuote: My clients aren't going to read about AGI in the papers, they'll just find their advice line is a robot.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old housing lawyer** at a small high-street firm acting for tenants.
He lives with his girlfriend Lena, a **teacher**, and uses AI tools now and then.
His steady worry is **legal aid** funding and a firm that depends on one ageing partner.
In fast AGI he expects to **lose his job**; with more time he moves toward **advocacy**.
He campaigns for a right to a **human lawyer** and a public legal service.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time for him and no lawyer for his **clients**.
whatWouldHelp: A legal right to a **human lawyer** when a home is at stake.
